items.title: 14.3.1 The Cross Product or Vector Product of Two Vectors and its Geometrical Interpretation

blocks.text: One of the key multiplication operations involving vectors in space is the cross product. Unlike the dot product, which results in a scalar, the cross product of two vectors yields a vector quantity. The vector product is widely used in Physics, particularly in fields, mechanics and electricity. It is only defined for vectors in space.

Let \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) be two non-zero vectors. The cross or vector product of \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) gives a vector that is perpendicular to both the vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\), written as \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\), is defined by

blocks.text_alt: u cross v equals (modulus of u times modulus of v times sine theta) times n

blocks.text: where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors, such that \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\) and \(\underline{n}\) is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) with direction given by the right-hand rule.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read the definition in two parts:
1. Magnitude (size): \(|\underline{u} \times \underline{v}| = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\), because \(|\underline{n}| = 1\). Since \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\), \(\sin\theta \ge 0\), so this size is never negative.
2. Direction: the unit vector \(\underline{n}\), perpendicular to the plane containing \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\). A plane has two perpendicular directions (up and down); the right hand rule tells us which one to take.
Why only in space? A direction perpendicular to two vectors lying in a plane must leave that plane, so it needs the third dimension.

blocks.alt: Two panels. Figure (a): vectors u and v from a point O in a shaded plane with angle theta between them; the unit vector n and the vector u cross v point straight up from O; a right hand with the thumb up, fingers curling from u towards v. Figure (b): vectors u and v in a plane; n and v cross u point straight down; a right hand with the thumb down.
blocks.caption: Figure (a): direction of u × v; Figure (b): direction of v × u, by the right hand rule (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

items: (i) If the fingers of the right hand point along the vector \(\underline{u}\) and then curl towards the vector \(\underline{v}\), then the thumb will give the direction of \(\underline{n}\) which is \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\). It is shown in the figure (a).
(ii) In figure (b), the right hand rule shows the direction of \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to apply the rule, step by step:
1. Put \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) tail to tail (starting from the same point).
2. Point the fingers of your RIGHT hand along the first vector \(\underline{u}\).
3. Curl the fingers towards the second vector \(\underline{v}\) through the smaller angle \(\theta\).
4. The thumb now points along \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\).
For \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) you start from \(\underline{v}\) and curl towards \(\underline{u}\): the hand turns over and the thumb points the opposite way. Same size, opposite direction. So the order of the vectors in a cross product matters.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick size example (ours): if \(|\underline{u}| = 3\), \(|\underline{v}| = 4\) and \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\), then
\[|\underline{u} \times \underline{v}| = 3 \cdot 4 \cdot \sin 30^{\circ}\]
\[= 12 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = 6\]
and \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) points perpendicular to the plane of \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\), on the side given by the right hand rule.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = (|\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta)\,\underline{n}\), with \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\).
2. \(\underline{n}\) is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\).
3. Direction by the right hand rule: fingers along \(\underline{u}\), curl towards \(\underline{v}\), thumb gives \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\).
4. \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) has the same magnitude but the opposite direction.
5. \(|\underline{u} \times \underline{v}| = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\) is a non-negative number.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using the left hand: the rule works only with the right hand.
2. Curling from \(\underline{v}\) to \(\underline{u}\) when \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) is asked: always start from the first vector.
3. Writing \(\cos\theta\) (dot product) instead of \(\sin\theta\) in the cross product.
4. Forgetting \(\underline{n}\): without it \(|\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\) is only the magnitude, not the vector.
